subtopic: SALARIES OF PROFESSIONAL AND TECHNICAL OFFICIALS

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. II. H. STEVENS (Vancouver Centre): Might I ask the Minister of Finance whether the government are yet ready to announce the names of certain distinguished gentlemen who, they indicated a few days ago, would be asked to counsel with them regarding the duties, rates of salaries and so forth in connection with technical employees in the service?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALARIES OF PROFESSIONAL AND TECHNICAL OFFICIALS
speechtext:
I anticipated that this question might be asked, because my hon. friend had asked it before. As hon. members know, it has been represented that the remuneration provided in the government service is no longer attractive to persons of superior technical and professional training. The report made last year by the Civil Service Commission recommends a graduated flat increase of from $240 to $420 per annum. This would apply to 1,936 persons, and involves $690,000 to one class and $60,000 to another, or a total of $750,000.
While there may be those who feel that, generally speaking, the civil servants of Canada are as well provided for in the way of salaries as are their fellow citizens who furnish the revenues to pay for the services, it is felt that in the public interest a fair comparison of salaries within and without the service should be available. The government,
therefore, invited Mr. E. W. Beatty, president and chairman of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, Sir George Garneau, of Garneau Limitee, Quebec city, and Doctor Murray, president of the university of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon, to inquire into and report on these phases, thereby providing the government with information permitting a readjustment fair to all interested.
May I add that the government feel that this house will agree the country is fortunate in being able to secure the services of men of such wide experience.

Mr. Speaker, as I understand that it
is the intention of the government when the house goes into supply to enter upon a discussion of the estimates of the post office department, I thought that this might be an appropriate time to enter upon a brief discussion of the question of rural mail contracts as they now exist in the Dominion of Canada. When I heard at noon to-day that this matter was coming up, I notified the secretary of the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) that I proposed to discuss this matter, and I intend before I resume my seat to move an amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is rather late, without notice.

I gave notice. The
amendment which I propose to move is one which I believe will bring on a general discussion of the matter and in the end lead to action by the government. It is not a subject which is in any way new to the House of Commons or to the present Postmaster General or to the government, because on three or four occasions in the past five or six years this matter has been fairly well discussed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:

a copy of the amendment.

I will give my right hon. friend a copy. So the matter which I intend to lay before the house on this occasion cannot in any way be considered as a new one. The truth is that a condition exists in regard to rural mail couriers in Canada to-day which is nothing less than a public scandal. It was about twenty years ago when we in Canada decided to establish a system of rural mail delivery throughout all the better settled portions of rural Canada. A system had been established prior to that time in the United States, and the experience in that country in regard to the delivery of rural mails throughout a very extended territory had been

Rural Mail Contracts-Mr. Guthrie
pretty satisfactory. We launched the experiment in Canada with some trepidation, I remember, but gradually we have extended the system through the better settled portions of rural Canada until to-day we have in operation, as I understand, some 4,007 rural mail routes which are of great benefit and convenience to our rural population.
The system which was adopted in the first instance in regard to these rural mail routes was one based on tender and contract. Certain routes were publicly advertised, tenders were called, and as a rule a fairly large number of tenderers responded to the advertisement in the hope of securing occupation as mail carriers in the rural parts of Canada. I suppose that lack of experience had something to do with the unsatisfactory conditions which attended the first tenders and the first contracts, but. as time has gone on,, conditions instead of improving have gradually become worse until to-day we find a system established throughout practically the whole length and breadth of this country under which certain men who are practically employees of this government and of this country, for the purpose of carrying His Majesty's mails, are not receiving an adequate return for the services they perform. Indeed, so inadequate is the return to our rural mail couriers that the matter has become nothing less than a public scandal. Year after year this matter has 'been brought to the attention of this government and of the present Postmaster General during the discussion of the Post Office estimates. Year after year the rural letter carriers have requested that their claims be considered and that they be treated on some fairer basis and on some higher standard than anything they have enjoyed hitherto.
Now, the situation I will briefly describe as follows. The figures which I give, it must be understood, will be only average figures; I cannot go into particular cases; but I find that in the report of the Postmaster General for the year ending March 31, 1928, the total cost to the Dominion for the " conveyance of mails by ordinary land" is $6,291,180.52. I have been informed by officials in the Post Office department that this item includes the cost of all the rural mail routes, of all the stage routes, and all the routes known as station-to-post office routes; these are all referred to under one item as " conveyance of mails by ordinary land." Just what part of that single item is devoted to the delivery of rural mail I am unable to say with precision; I can only form an estimate, but information has 'been given to me that the number of established routes to-day is 4,007, and it has been represented that the average
route in Canada at the present time is one of twenty miles. Some routes are a little more than this, some a little less, but as an average twenty miles is supposed to be about right. The average pay for a courier who travels that route of twenty miles is, according to my informant in the department, about $800, although according to a statement which I have received from the Letter Carriers Association the average amount which each carrier receives is only $720. I am taking the higher figure of $800 for a twenty-mile route, which would be payment to the courier at the rate of $40 per mile over a period of a year.
Now, what is he supposed to do for that money? In the first place, he has to maintain the service and in most, if not all, cases the service has to be daily; he has to perform his trip in all kinds and conditions of weather, winter and summer, with few, if any, holidays-I believe there are one or two holidays specified now; he has to maintain a sufficient horse and conveyance to cover his route, and he has to maintain himself and his family, all out of that average sum of $800 which he receives as a total annual remuneration.
One has only to state these facts to demonstrate that a service based upon such unfair conditions can only result in one thing -a public scandal. No man can perform^ the service1 satisfactorily under such conditions. The maintenance of the horse and equipment takes more than half of the remuneration which he receives. Officials in the Post Office department tell me that in order to ensure proper service on a twenty-mile route, two horses are necessary. I know of routes upon which only one horse is maintained. But take it, if you will, at only one horse, the first question is: what does it cost to keep a horse in Canada to-day ? I have made inquiries from men who ought to know-some men in this house, some outside-and I find that for the maintenance of one horse there is annually required:

Or $440 on any route that requires two horses-and the majority of them do. _ I submit these figures to the house as the minimum figures which I have been able to obtain. The figures supplied by the Letter Carriers Association are far in advance of these figures. They tell me that three tons of hay is far too

Rural Mail Contracts-Mr. Guthrie
little to maintain a horse for a year, and that $13 a ton is too low a price; that $20 is too little for horseshoeing, and that $40 is too little for depreciation and repairs of the equipment. But I am taking these as minimum figures which show that a mail carrier will have an actual outlay, if he employs two horses, of $440 for maintenance. This will leave him only $360 for the support of himself, and of his family.
There is no man in this country who can support himself and his family on $360; it cannot be done. Is not that a very strong reason why there is such vigorous and persistent complaint in regard to this matter? These men are underpaid while performing a very important service. Their net remuneration is but $360. Why, the figures supplied to this house by the Department of Labour show that the minimum requirement for a family of five in January of the present year was $1,122.60, for the mere necessaries of life. And yet under present conditions as operating throughout this Dominion the Post Office department we are asking these couriers of His Majesty's mail in the rural districts to do their work for $360 a year. Mr. Speaker, I repeat it cannot be done. The men are losing money. They are suffering grave hardship. Surely it is beneath the dignity of such a country as Canada, it is beneath the dignity of any government, to allow a system of that kind to continue.
Now, what will the result be? Loss to the contractors? Certainly. Inefficiency in the service? Certainly. Dishonesty will probably follow. Indeed there are some parts of Ontario where the matter has become a real scandal. There have been prosecutions before magistrates by humane societies at various points because these contractors for the conveyance of His Majesty's mails have not had money enough to feed t'heir horses. The magistrates have taken a lenient view of these cases and have dismissed them, but the matter has become an outstanding scandal.
What is the real difficulty? The tender system, I submit, is a wrong system in regard to this matter. When it was first introduced some twenty years ago it was experimental. We had had no experience at that time. But why continue it when we know year in and year out that the system is not satisfactory and is causing grave hardship? Why allow the matter to remain as it is year after year when it has been pointed out in this house, on every occasion on which post office estimates are discussed, that the system is unfair, that it is a gross hardship, and that it must be altered and improved? Why does the government delay action in this matter?

What is the system which has been adopted in the United States, for instance? There they began with a system of tender and contract for specified routes. They found it unworkable, just as we have found it unworkable and unsatisfactory in Canada. But in the United States they promptly changed it; they put it on the mileage basis. There they have established certain definite routes, the mileage is calculated, and a man is appointed as letter carrier on a route with the definite understanding that he shall receive so much per mile. I believe there is some variation allowed in prices by reason of physical difficulties which may arise in the country over which the courier has to travel. In the United States at the present time the courier receives in the majority of cases $75 per mile travelled. This is not an unreasonable amount; it is, I submit, fair and reasonable. It may be that the United States rate at the present time would be too high in a country such as Canada where distances may be greater and population sparser. But $40 a mile which is the average they are receiving now, is absurd. Something must be done to increase the amount, and steps must be taken to make these men permanent. Forty dollars a mile is the average in Canada and $75 in the United States. Moreover, our system lacks the permanence which attaches to the system in the United States. When a mail contract is let, and when the local community start tendering one against another, they cut the figure down and down to rock bottom, and the contract is given for four years to the lowest man provided the contractor can furnish the necessary security for the carrying out of the contract. But at the end of the four years he finds that he cannot make money. Indeed, a good many of them are willing to give it up, but unfortunately they have their horses and their equipment and do not know what to do in the matter. If they do not renew the contract at practically the same amount there is another advertisement for tenders, with another group of tenderers. Other people know what the former contractor got and they try to cut a little bit under him. And they do so. The result is that the figures have been going down and down and down, while the cost of living has been going up or has been maintained at a very high standard; and so the system has been positively disastrous to many men.
Now what we ask by this motion and what we have asked for the last three or four sessions in this house, is that a new system be adopted forthwith. The mileage system should be adopted in place of the tender system and the positions should be made permanent, just as permanent as are letter

Rural Mail Contracts-Mr. Guthrie
carriers in the city districts. An amount should be fixed as remuneration having regard to the	cost of living in this
country and the duties and responsibilities of the courier. I do not suggest the rate which they now pay in the United States, but I do suggest S70 or at any rate $60 a mile as a reasonable sum in this country. Now, assuming that the present contractors do average $800 a year each, and assuming that there are 4,000 rural mail routes, this involves an annual expenditure to-day of $3,200,000 or thereabouts of the $6,000,000 item which is in the Postmaster General's report. That is on the basis	of $40	a mile. What
would be the effect of increasing the rate to S60 a mile-a 50 per cent increase? You would raise the total amount by $1,600,000. Would not that be fair? Instead of $3,200,000, which I assume it is now approximately-I cannot give the figures definitely-it would increase to $4,800,000 a year; and if you deemed proper to make it $70 a mile, which I submit would be reasonable, you would need to add another 25 per cent to the last figure I have given.
I submit that under present conditions in Canada it is not beyond this Dominion to grant $70 a mile, and I also submit that the tender system should be abolished at once. In imy opinion the position of rural mail courier should be made permanent immediately, and a definite satisfactory amount should be fixed as remuneration upon the mileage basis. This is not a new proposal in this house, nor is it in the country. The public conscience has been aroused throughout the Dominion in regard to this matter. The press of the country, without distinction politically, has discussed the matter editorially, and as briefly as possible I am going to put on Hansard with my remarks some press comments to show that there is no political bias in the matter to it, to show also that the men now engaged as rural mail carriers in Canada have a real and substantial grievance. And I ask again why this government has not remedied this grievance before now. Listen to what the Toronto Globe says. I read from a Globe editorial of September 10, 1928:
The annual meeting of the Canadian Mail Contractors' Association, held in Toronto the other day. brought once more to the attention of the public the, unfortunate conditions under which the rural mail contractor carries on his work. Chief among the resolutions passed by the carriers was that requesting the government to abolish the present _ contract plan under which mail is delivered in the country, and to bring about the introduction of the salary system on the basis of $70 per mile per year for rural contractors. The request made by these men is reasonable. What they
are asking from the government is simply a living wage and to be placed on a similar footing to the postal carriers in the cities of the Dominion.	_	.
The contract system has outlived its usefulness, and should be discarded without delay. Tt was given up long ago by the United States government, and the rural mail men placed on the same basis as other employees of the postal department. The contract system in vogue in Canada has little to commend it, except that it is cheap. The man who submits the lowest tender may get the job. Too often it may happen that he will also perform the worst service. The rural mail carriers have protested for long against the present plan, and have petitioned the government repeatedly to have it changed. Surely the time has come when their plea should be heeded.
That from the Toronto Globe. The Ottawa Citizen has also spoken editorially, and its views are as follows:
A convincing ease has been made out for better treatment at the hands of the Department at Ottawa by the Rural Mail Contractors' Association in the memorandum they recently sent to members of both houses of parliament. As most persons are aware, rural mail deliveries are carried out under a contract system whereby the contractor undertakes to deliver mail along a given route for four years. The average length of a mail contract route is 20 miles and the average yearly contract price paid by the government is $732. Besides furnishing wholly inadequate remuneration for the character of the work and duties entailed, this system possesses inherent defects which only its abolition can remove. The rural mail men point out that the average upkeep of a contractor's horses and rigs during the last five years has been $1,058.
That is more than twice the figure I gave.
This means an average loss of $326 yearly, in addition to which the mail contractor has given his time and assumed responsibilities free of charge.
The London Advertiser has a long article very much to the same effect which I need not quote. The Toronto Star contains a very strong article against the present system, calling on the government to change it at once. The Montreal Herald too carries a strong article, and comments appear in the Telegraph-Journal of St. John, the Hamilton Herald, the Canadian Countryman, the St. Thomas Times and Journal, the Farmers' Sun, the Hamilton Spectator, the Stratford Beacon-Herald-in fact one may say all the leading newspapers of Canada have brought this matter to the attention of the Postmaster General and the government, yet year after year nothing has been done. There is a way, however, by which I hope to bring the question pointedly to the notice of the Postmaster General and by which I propose to ask the house to deal with it. I am moving a motion on going into supply this afternoon which, as the house knows, is always in the

Rural Mail Contracts-Mr. Kaiser
nature of a motion of want of confidence. I have taken that course in order to test out this matter in this House of Commons. In years past many hon. members in various quarters of the house have discussed this matter very forcibly; they have laid before us the case of the rural mail couriers with great effect, and I sincerely hope that upon this occasion they will implement the speeches they made in this house in previous years. I hope that as a result of this vote these rural mail couriers who have been complaining for years and who have been suffering gross injustice for years, will have their injuries remedied as they should have been remedied by this government long ago.
This afternoon I have briefly stated the case to the house as I believe it to exist, and I have drawn up a resolution expressing as weli as I can what is in my mind. I may say in connection with this resolution, however- and I say this in the presence of my leader- that it embodies the policy of the Conservative party on this question, and if the Conservative party is returned to power this policy as outlined in this amendment will be carried out without further delay.
Wiith these remarks, Mr. Speaker, I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens):
That all the words after the word "that" in the motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house the present system of awarding contracts for the delivery of rural mail by tender has proved unfair, burdensome and unsatisfactory, and that such rural mail carriers should be appointed by the Civil Service Commission upon a permanent basis with a definite rate of pay, based upon mileage and the physical conditions of the territory involved, having regard to the amount paid to the other servants of the government for similar employment."

Mr. Speaker, the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has drawn the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) and of this house to a long standing grievance on the part of a large body of faithful and efficient public servants against whom there has been what might well be termed an unfair discrimination, in that, although discharging duties which are as important to the public as those performed by other servants who are on the permanent list and receive regular salaries, they are not similarly treated. Representations have been made from year to year on behalf of these mail carriers and facts have been cited which should long ago have brought about a remedy of this grievance. In fact, one wonders why there has been this continued neglect, this refusal on the part of the Postmaster General to consider the requests of this large body of public servants and to find a remedy. He has shown in some instances activity and keen interest on behalf of other employees of the department. In fact, he has taken pains to point out to the house that in some cases the Civil Service Commission have not met his views with respect to increases of salaries.
We all know the character of the duties of a rural mail carrier. They are exacting; they demand punctuality. He must be faithful; he must be on the job every day of the year, Sundays excepted, rain or shine, no matter whether the travelling is good or bad. He must furnish ample security for the discharge of his duties. He is under supervision, and in every respect his position is a difficult and an exacting one. I am sure the Postmaster General must recall the fact that from time to time members of parliament have to interview his deputy and those in charge of this service on behalf of unfortunates who have tendered for it only to find out that they have signed a contract binding them for a period of years, and that the proposition has been a losing one for them. In some cases they have had to ask to be relieved and have been replaced by others. Sometimes persons are found without knowledge of the situation who are willing to take over the contracts, but these unfortunate individuals soon find themselves in trouble. I know personally of contracts that have had to be transferred three or four times, in each case to the disadvantage and loss of the party who took it over.
We do not ask for tenders for similar services on the part of mail clerks or those
1618	COMMONS
Rural Mail Contracts-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
in the postal service, and I think the time is long past when we should continue this method. These ought to be considered permanent employees and there ought to be a reasonable, fixed compensation for them. Not knowing that the matter was going to come up in the house, I took the liberty some time ago to write to the postal department in Washington to find out how they dealt with the matter there, and under date of March 29, 1929, I received from the fourth assistant postmaster general a letter which I desire to put on Hansard. The letter reads:
My Dear Mr. Stewart:
Reference is made to your letter of March 23, requesting information as to the rate of pay of rural mail carriers in the United States, and as to particulars of the equipment and vehicles which they or the department provide for the service.
The salaries which rural carriers shall receive are fixed by law, being based on the length of the route served and the frequency of the deliveries, routes being served either daily except Sunday or three times a week. For serving a rural route of twenty-four miles six days in the week, the salary is $1,800 per annum; on routes twenty-two miles and less than twenty-four miles, $1,728; on routes twenty miles and less than twenty-two miles, $1,620; on routes eighteen miles, and less than twenty miles, $1,440; on routes sixteen miles and less than eighteen miles, $1,260; on routes fourteen miles and less than sixteen miles, $1,080; on routes twelve miles and less than fourteen miles, $1,008; on routes ten miles and less than twelve miles, $936; on routes eight miles and less than ten miles, $864; on routes six miles and less than eight miles, $792; on routes four miles and less than six miles, $720. Each rural carrier assigned to a route on which daily service is performed receives $30 per mile per annum for each mile of his route in excess of twenty-four miles or major fraction thereof, based on actual mileage, and each rural carrier assigned to a route on which triweekly service is performed receives $15 per mile for each mile of said route in excess of forty-eight miles or major fraction thereof, based on actual mileage.
A rural carrier who serves one tri-weekly route is paid a salary and equipment maintenance allowance on the basis of a route one-half of the length of the route served by him. A rural carrier serving two tri-weeldy routes is paid a salary and equipment maintenance allowance on the basis of a route one-half of the combined length of the two routes.
In addition to the salary' each carrier is paid an equipment maintenance in the sum of 4 cents per mile per day for each mile or major fraction of a mile scheduled.
Rural carriers are required to provide and to maintain suitable vehicles with which to perform the service.
It will foe seen that this is a very much more generous compensation than we allow for this service. I do not suggest that the situation requires that we should pay as much as they are paying in the United States, and it has occurred to me that I might make

I wish to make a few remarks in support of the resolution introduced by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). This question has been before the house on many occasions; it has come up almost every session for a great many years. In anything I have to say I am in no way criticising the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) because the system that prevails has been in existence for a number of years. We know that the rural mail delivery service is very efficient, and that the farmers of this country would not wish to do without it. It is a great improvement over the system prevailing before, when the people in the country had to drive many miles into the nearest village or town to get their mail. The rural mail couriers to-day not only carry the ordinary mail and registered mail, but also deliver small supplies to the farmers, and collect their mail for delivery to the post office.
I wish to direct the attention of the Postmaster General to a comparison between the remuneration paid to the rural mail couriers and that of the mail carriers in the cities. In my county there is a rural mail route of fifteen miles, for which the courier is paid $750 a year. That amounts to about $2.40 per trip. This man is compelled to keep two horses and a vehicle. He has to provide equipment throughout the year, meet the cost of all repairs and maintenance, and keep his family, all on $750 a year. His work on the route occupies the whole of his time, because the roads are bad and it takes him almost a whole day to make the trip. It costs him more than half of that $750 to maintain his horses and rig. He is on the road every day, six days in the week, and
has only six holidays throughout the year. In the performance of his duties he is out in all kinds of weather, rain or shine, cold or hot, and over all kinds of roads. I think the minister was not listening when I said that all this man received for his services on this route of fifteen miles was $750 a year, or about $2.40 a trip, and he has to supply the whole equipment. The government supplies nothing. His brother delivering mail in the city receives a minimum of about $1,080 a year, with the chance of advancing each year until he reaches a maximum of $1,500. In addition, he is provided with at least one suit of clothes, if not two, per year, and I think also his boots, and he has no equipment expenses of any kind. Of course he has his family to keep, but the man in the country has his family as well. There is no comparison between the amounts paid by way of remuneration for these two services, and I do not see how the Postmaster General can refuse to take into consideration the conditions under which the rural mail couriers work. Of course we know that they tender for the route and that generally the price is set by the man himself-but not always, because the system of tender is such that the tenderer is compelled to put in the lowest figure at which he thinks he can get the work. I know of cases where the inspector who opens the tenders has peddled them around amongst the different tenderers to see if he could not get a lower bid. That has been done more than once in the section from which I come.

That has been changed.
All the tenders are now sent to my department.

I am glad that change has been made, because I know that the practice prevailed some years ago. I hope the minister will take into consideration the comparison I have made between the remuneration of the mail carrier in the city and that of rural mail courier, and that the latter will receive better remuneration for the work they perform.
There is another point. At the end of four years, if these rural mail couriers wish to retain the route, they have to put in a new tender. If they do not carry on with the work they have their team and rig on their hands, and frequently they have no further use for them; consequently in many cases they put in a lower bid than they otherwise would have done. The average equipment, if it is anything like decent equipment, costs between two and four hundred dollars; in fact it is only very poor equipment that you can

There is precisely here a point which exemplifies the system. As I told the house last night, in the recess between six and eight o'clock I had to go through some sixty records of evidence, classifying them in alphabetical order, then taking the list of bills before the house and trying to ascertain which of the records of evidence corresponded with each bill. There is no indication whatever. These records are sent to us in groups without any indication of their relation each to the particular bill called when such legislation is before the house. This evening I happened to have an advantage over most other members in that I took a little time between six and eight to look into the records and I succeeded in marking about one half of them with letters corresponding to the bills to which they relate. Then, in the expectation that these bills would be called in their order, I began reading the evidence respecting the first bills likely to be taken up.
We were told last evening, and I think quite properly, by such hon. gentlemen-to mention only two-as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan)- two hon. gentlemen who, I think I may say without exaggeration, are shining lights in parliament and in Canada with regard to judicial and legal matters-that in respect of the question now before us we in this house are acting as the highest court of justice in the land. These hon. gentlemen have told us that, parliament having seen fit to establish no jurisdiction respecting divorce in either the province of Ontario or the province of Quebec, parliament itself acts as the highest court of justice in Canada, and that therefore it is the duty of every hon. member of this house to take with respect to these bills the attitude of a judge or of a juror. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, whose personal views I well know and to whose sense of duty as well as his dignity I can testify, regarding him both as a public man and as a friend, compared our position to that of judges in his own native province of Nova Scotia, where courts of divorce have been established and have exercised jurisdiction for many years. It has been said that in this matter we act as a court of appeal; that by common consent and usage a committee of parliament performs-rather, I should say, now, committees perform-the duty of a court of inquiry; they find the facts and, it is said, all that we have to do is to ratify, so to speak, their judgment. But I do not think it has been suggested by anyone, either by the leader of the opposition or by any of the other legal members of this house, that we can pass final judgment in the matter, conscientiously and with intelligence, without at least knowing the evidence. One hon. member on the other side of the house has made the statement that it takes a very short time to read the evidence, that in about fifteen minutes any one of these records can be read. He went further and said that in the committee of the senate it took about twenty-five minutes for that court of inquiry to hear the witnesses, to hear the pleas of lawyers and to render their judgment. In other words, in twenty-five minutes a committee of one of the branches of this highest court of justice in the land declares that a marriage is null. That is the position and we as a court of review, a court of appeal or, if you prefer it, as a ratifying body passing final judgment upon the findings of a committee of the senate, come here to decide upon these cases. A bill is called and it stands; another bill is called and it stands, a third bill is called and stands and so we come to the fifth or the sixth on the list. Who has the time to read the records and the evidence in the six bills which may be called within two minutes? We are told that it is our duty to place our stamp of ratification on the findings of the court of inquiry, the divorce committee of the other branch of parliament. I appeal seriously to the other members of this house; whatever title we give ourselves, whether we call ourselves a parliament, whether we call ourselves one-half of that so-called high tribunal, or whether we style ourselves a court of review which revises and passes final judgment upon the findings of the other branch, can we do so without knowing upon what we must adjudicate? Mr. Speaker, as I understand the position taken by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), he is arguing that we should not discuss the merits of this particular bill at this stage; that that should be done when the report comes from the private bills committee. What we are discussing now is the principle of divorce. I attempted to convey to the house yesterday the terrible extent to which the evil of divorce had been scattered throughout the Dominion, not only by the action of the provincial legislatures which created divorce courts, but by the actions of this parliament as well. But that is only a part of the harm which is being done. There are a number of people -who do not dare to face public opinion in Canada by coming to parliament or to the provincial courts in order to obtain divorce, but who go beyond our borders and secure divorce elsewhere. I have under my hand the official statistics furnished by the Department of Trade and Commerce, Dominion Bureau of Statistics, and I wish to read the following paragraph showing the extent to which divorce has spread in Canada. Last year 785 divorces were granted in Canada by the courts and the Dominion parliament. This is what the Dominion Bureau of Statistics says:
Divorces granted in the United States to persons married in Canada.
A fact which throws considerable new light on the divorce situation in Canada is found in the Marriage and Divorce Bulletin of the United States Bureau of the Census. The statistics of this publication indicate the surprisingly large extent to which divorces are granted in that country to persons married in Canada. Thus, in 1922, no fewer than 1,368 divorce decrees were granted to couples married in Canada, a number more than two and one-half times as large as the total number granted in Canada in the same year. This number also formed 36.2 per cent of the number of divorces granted in United States during the year to couples married in foreign countries, while, at the same time the percentage of the Canadian-born population to the total foreign-born amounted to only 8.1 per cent. The Bulletin goes on to say; "It is possible that many Canadians acquire a residence in the United States for the sole purpose of obtaining divorce because, in general, divorce laws are more liberal in the United States than in Canada." Of the 1,368 divorces granted in 1922 to couples who had been married in Canada, no fewer than 462 were granted by the courts of the state of Michigan, while 135 were granted by the courts of the state of Washington and 128 in California. No later figures than the above have been published in connection with the dissolution of marriages contracted outside the United States.
Those who read the Montreal papers may have noticed last week o-r the week before that a judge held that Canadians married in Canada cannot obtain a divorce in the United
States and then come back to this country and imagine that their divorce is valid here. According to the findings of that judge people who are married in Canada can have their marriage annulled only in Canada if they intend to remain citizens of this country. We find ourselves in the position of having hundreds and, perhaps before long, thousands of Canadians who, not wishing to go through the very unpleasant ordeal of bringing up their cases before the senate or the provincial courts, go into a foreign country, secure a divorce there and return to Canada. The number of marriages being dissolved is such a serious matter that, to use a French expression, malgre nous, in spite of ourselves, we are obliged to deal with the problem of divorce. I hope the time will come when the public in Canada will realize the deplorable state of affairs and take some action in the matter. I have conscientious objections to divorce, but I hope the day is fast coming when members elected by the public will realize that the present state of affairs is beyond common sense and that means must be found to end it.
It has been said that the fathers of confederation did not impose divorce either on Ontario or on Quebec. There were originally four provinces in the confederation. Divorce existed in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick prior to confederation and, that being the case, they had to provide in the constitution for that condition. They put it under federal jurisdiction on the ground that the federal parliament would be more difficult of access and the procedure more costly, the result, being that divorce would be discouraged. They were right at the time, because in the first ten years after confederation only seven divorces were granted, whereas we have reached 293 during the present session. Of course public opinion in Canada has somewhat changed in regard to this question. The official bulletin ascribes that to the war and the consequences of the war.' That may be true, or it may not; but what is happening in Canada is happening unfortunately in all countries, and, while not wanting to make any criticism, I can only repeat and urge that the position we now occupy is a false one, because the hearing of these witnesses occurs in the senate, whereas the House of Commons as represented by its private bills committee does not see the witnesses or hear the evidence. There are now on the order paper forty-one divorce bills which stand for second reading and seventeen that have been read the first time at this sitting. Is this the way the parliament of Canada is going to act-

Procedure Respecting Divorce
to dissolve seventy or seventy-five marriages in perhaps a few minutes, throw the children out on the street and give to the guilty party the same privilege that we give to the innocent party? Our sympathies naturally go with the innocent party, but by the second clause which we insert in the divorce bill we give the guilty party the right to marry again; the result of our judgment is inevitable.
Nobody objects to a judicial separation provided that it is properly carried out. That is the law we have in the province of Quebec under clause 185 of the code, and separations take place daily. Alimony is provided for the wife and proper care is taken of the children. But in this case nothing of the kind happens; we simply break the marriage tie and put the guilty party on the same footing as the innocent party. If we were to remove the Second clause from these bills, that is the clause authorizing the people to re-marry, I do not think you would have ten per cent of the applications you have at the present time.
Therefore I can only repeat what I said yesterday, namely, that I am conscientiously opposed to divorce; I am opposed to it for the stronger reason now that it has become the greatest problem we have to deal with in this country. What will it be in five or ten years from now unless some means are devised to stop it? The only way we can stop it is to make it as difficult as possible to obtain divorce and, when it is granted, it should be granted in an equitable manner so that the innocent party will be treated differently from the guilty.

Mr. Speaker, I doubt if there is any more exacting responsibility in the public service of this Dominion than is involved in the carrying of His Majesty's mail, and I also doubt whether that responsibility is discharged under any greater handicap than obtains in the rural districts. As the mover of the amendment (Mr. Guthrie) has stated, the change proposed has to do not with a theory but with a recognized condition. The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) has suggested that the amendment is prompted merely by political expediency. I submit, sir, it is quite apparent that the government of the day, while opposing the change now, will as a matter of political opportunism incorporate it in their preelection budget next session.
It does seem to me that throughout the various provinces it is recognized that this change should be made. It has been sponsored by those who sit to your left, Mr. Speaker, and it should be adopted by those
who sit to your right. Everyone familiar with rural conditions realizes the handicap under which the rural mail carriers serve the department. Those of us who travel the highways and byways of the Dominion recognize that the average rural mail carrier is not a very good advertisement for the Postmaster General's department. The rattle of his dilapidated buggy and the stagger of his poor lame and blind horse are familiar intimations that approaching you is the rural mail carrier, one of the servants of the Postmaster General.
I have had some experience in feeding cheap horses and also in feeding horses cheaply, and I am in a position to state that even for the figures quoted by the hon. member for South Wellington a horse cannot be maintained in reasonably fit condition for the mail carrying service. To show that the figures I am about to give the house are reasonable, I ask the indulgence of hon. members while I go into details. It has been admitted that a mail carrier needs two horses. I submit that $100 is a reasonable price per horse. That represents $200, the interest on which would be $12, at 6 per cent. The cost of feed, hay and oats at present prices, at the country point, would be $150 each, or $300 per annum. And then there is the depreciation in regard to each horse, because I submit that no horse can stand a rural mail service on rough country roads for a longer period than five years, so that depreciation can safely and sanely be estimated at S20 per horse, or $40 per annum for the two. As regards horse shoeing-and many times the horse would have to go unshod-I would estimate $25 each, or $50 per annum for the pair. Then interest, depreciation and repairs in connection with the vehicle, together with blankets and general equipment, would represent another $30. This brings the total to $432, as the minimum expenditure which the rural mail carrier in Canada must incur. Now if the first estimate which has been given of the amount the mail carrier receives-$720 -is correct, it would leave him $290 or less than a dollar a day; while if the second estimate is correct-$800-he is left with $370 per annum or $1.25 per day. Perhaps those with large families receive the second rate, $800. I wish to point out that this is a ridiculous state of affairs in the public service of this Dominion. We have been told that the messengers in this house, who merely stand at attention and wait for someone to tell them what to do, receive $4 a day. Yet here are men who are obliged to drive up and down this country in all sorts of weather, on stormy days, every day of the week but Sunday,

travelling frequently through blizzards, over snowdrifts and through muddy roads. And this is the remuneration they get for loyal service to an important branch of the public service.
Not only are the rural mail carriers expecting relief in this matter, but they are entitled to it, and it seems to me that the people of Canada would approve of this increased expenditure especially in view of the fact that this government, though it preaches economy, is spending money to beautify this city and at the same time is increasing the salaries of deputy ministers, securing new automobiles-some members of the government take their cars with them wherever they go-and expending money in other directions. These are the apostles of economy, the friends of the poor man; yet they cannot pay a reasonable remuneration to men who are engaged in this important work and who are rendering just as loyal service as any other employees in the government. Surely it is high time that these rural mail carriers were given some consideration. It is not a joke or a gesture, as the hon. member for Quebec South has suggested. We are faced here with a very real problem. These men find themselves in a situation where it is impossible for them to keep their wives and families on the wages paid by the Postmaster General's department. For these reasons I submit that the motion proposed by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) is fully warranted, and I appeal to the government to consider the matter favourably and to give to the rural carriers their just recompense for the splendid service they are rendering the whole Dominion.

In rising to speak to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) I wish to refer to the first remark he made. He said that I had been notified of his intention to move this amendment. I received word of his intention at a quarter to three this afternoon, and in conversation with my assistant secretary, who got the word, I was told-I think that this perhaps was a misunderstanding-that the hon. member would deal with the question of railway mail clerks. Receiving that word at a quarter to three I immediately undertook to obtain all the information possible touching the situation and the salaries of railway mail clerks. I do not wish to offer as an excuse the short notice given with respect to this amendment; but I think that when an amendment of this importance is to come up, an amendment which involves if adopted

an additional expenditure from the treasury of this Dominion of some $7,000,000 a year, a little more time by way of notice should be given to the person who has charge of the department which has to make the expenditure.
However, I have had an opportunity of listening to the speeches which have been made here this afternoon and evening, and while I am not going to say that our rural mail carriers are paid sufficient and might not be paid more, at the same time I wish to point out that the hon. member in proposing the amendment chose to deal only with rural mail deliverers, so to speak, because he directed his argument entirely to the 4.007 rural mail routes in Canada. He forgot altogether to deal with the six or seven thousand other mail carriers who do not deliver mail at rural boxes. If my hon. friend wanted to be fair-or whoever coached him and gave him the information on which he based his argument-he would not have overlooked that other class of hard working mail deliverers in Canada amounting to some 6,000.
Who are they?

Exactly; I thought the
question would be asked, and it shows that my hon. friend opposite does not know what he is talking about. There are 4,007 persons employed delivering mail on rural mail routes where there are boxes in which they can place the mail addressed to residents of those districts; and there are about 6,000 other mail contractors who use what we call the stage coach for delivery from post office to post office.
Who told you that?

My hon. friends opposite have not posted themselves on the subject, and undoubtedly they have ignored these people. Let me point out that these people draw from the treasury of the Dominion the nice little sum of $1,550,000 for that service. They are pretty well paid, and if the hon. gentleman who moved the amendment had added that sum to the amount that we paid to those who deliver mail in the boxes on the rural routes he would not have arrived at the average he gave in making his comparison with the amount paid by the United States government. He would have obtained a much higher average; he would have found that with this addition we are not so far behind the United States in this regard.
Let me give some figures in this connection. Rural mail delivery is the delivery of mail to boxes along the mail routes established throughout the Dominion of Canada. Of

Rural Mail Contracts-Mr. Veniot
these there are now 4,007, which number is increasing every year; I think 182 routes were added during the past year, and this service costs $2,825,317. If we were to pay a rate of $70 per mile, which hon. gentlemen say is the average paid under the monthly or yearly salaries in the United States, that would cost us $4,977,905. Stage services cost $1,550,000; under this new system which has been advocated they would cost $3,153,430. City services are on the same basis and include the delivery of mails from stations to post offices.
That is done by your own department.

That is not done by the department; it is done under contract. That shows that the hon. gentleman does not know what he is talking about. We ask for tenders and contracts are given under those tenders. That service costs us $720,000; if it were carried on under the monthly salary advocated by hon. gentlemen opposite the cost would jump to $2,160,000. Then we have our side services from the railway stations to the post offices throughout the entire Dominion of Canada, and those services cost $1,050,000. If they were placed on the basis of a monthly or yearly salary that cost would increase to $3,150,000. In other words, under the basis advocated by hon. gentlemen opposite the cost for the services rendered in Canada would be $13,441,335 as against the present cost of $6,145,317, or a total increase of $7,296,018. These figures cannot be contradicted; they have been worked out to a nicety. Last year I made a similar statement with regard to the difference in cost, but at that time I did not give these details.
Then there is another feature in connection with this agitation; I think that word correctly describes it, although I do not wish to apply it to hon. gentlemen opposite. This agitation was started by a certain person in Canada who is making a living by going around and advocating the adoption in this country of the United States system. Now he is advocating that if this system be adopted it be made retroactive to 1917, and to show the folly of that argument let me point out that such action would mean an expenditure of $87,522,216. That is all that gentleman wants. This man is not even a mail carrier; he calls himself secretary of the mail contractors' or mail carriers' association of Canada. Everyone has heard him plead his case and everyone knows he is urging the mail carriers throughout Canada to carry on this agitation.
Let me point out that I have been considering this question since it was first brought to my attention, which I think was in the winter of 1928. Looking over the whole system as it exists in Canada to-day, Mr. Speaker, I believe hon. gentlemen will believe me when I say that this system cannot be reviewed in one or even two years. It will take time to attempt to work out something which will better these conditions, if they can be bettered, but let me say that Canada never can adopt the system in force in the United States, because of our sparsely settled districts. The United States, with the population much more concentrated, can do that which we could not undertake in Canada on the same basis. Let me go further:	In
attempting to make that review, at one time I did think it might be a good thing to try to arrange what might be called a minimum tender, after looking over the whole situation and getting all the information required. That would not do away with the tender system but it would provide that no tender below the minimum would be considered by the department. It may be said that now we can refuse a tender if we consider it to be too low, -but that is not the case under the postal act, which provides that we must accept the lowest tender offered. Therefore, after reviewing the whole situation in order to see if a better system might be evolved, it may become necessary to ask for an amendment to the postal act, but I fear that if I should ask for that amendment immediately hon. gentlemen opposite would say that I wanted to play politics and handle the contracts for mail service as I saw fit. There is a great deal of merit in what he has stated regarding the pay that the rural mail carriers are receiving, and I do not think he has overstated the case. In many cases the rural mail carriers are underpaid, and I am glad to hear from the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) that he has been giving the matter consideration and that he intends to endeavour to arrive at some rate or some minimum salary that will meet the situation in some w-ay. But at the present time he is prevented under the act from doing so, and as we all know, the contracts can be renewed to the present carriers only at the existing rate of pay. It is also quite true that when tenders are invited, a large number of tenders are sent in and in many cases the present carriers ask that their contracts be renewed at the same rate and that the route be not put up for tender. I cannot quite agree with the argument that is sometimes advanced that this shows that the men are satisfied. On the contrary, I think it is quite true they are afraid that if they do not accept the contract at existing rates, they will lose the contract and that it will go to someone else. Therefore, rather than lose it, they are willing to enter into a new one at the same rate of pay. In the notice that is sent out there is a provision which reads:
In this connection, I might remind you that while the Post Office Act empowers the Postmaster General to renew existing contracts for further terms, such renewals can be executed only on existing terms and conditions.
Until the act is amended it is impossible for the Postmaster General to enter into any sort of arrangement other than is provided for in the act.

to carry on the country's business. It is a want of confidence motion, and I do not propose to be put in the position of not explaining my position clearly on this matter.
In our province we have in our rural service as fine a class of drivers as can be found anywhere in this Dominion, and they give us splendid service. It may be a surprise to my hon. friends to know that right in my home district where I have lived the best part of my life one of the first rural mail routes in the whole Dominion was established, and now the system has spread throughout the whole province so that to-day there is not one part of the province that is not served by rural mail delivery. We have a splendid service and as fine a class of men as can be found anywhere, and we would be only too glad to see them get an increase in salary if that is possible. But I shall be compelled to vote against tlhe amendment-for what reason? Because it is a want of confidence motion, and it cannot bring the relief which my hon. friend from South Wellington would like to lead the country to believe he desires to bring to the mail couriers under his motion. I therefore propose to vote against his amendment and to support the motion of the Minister of Finance that the house go into committee of supply and vote the money to carry on the public services of this country.

I was not in the house when the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) made his address this afternoon, but after listening to the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) I have sent over for the amendment, and I think the Postmaster General has not stuck to the text. The amendment reads:
In the opinion of this house the present system of awarding contracts for the delivery of rural mail by tender has proved unfair, burdensome and unsatisfactory, and that such rural mail carriers should be appointed by the Civil Service Commission upon a permanent basis with a definite rate of pay, based upon mileage and the physical conditions of the territory involved, having regard to the amount paid to the other servants of the government for similar employment.
Now, I can scarcely be accused of being a recent convert to this proposed change, because the first time that I addressed this house I did what I could to bring to the attention of hon. members the unfair condition under which the rural mail carriers were working and the inadequate remuneration they were receiving. I think the Postmaster General is evading the question in asking why did not the previous government take care of this matter between 1911 and 1921. The Post-

master General was no doubt in this country during that time, and he must not forget that the war was followed by a very trying period of reorganization and rehabilitation. I do not think any unfair advantage was taken of him, because he had been having interviews from time to time with the Rural Mail Carriers Association. And, Mr. Speaker, I see no reason why the rural mail carriers of this country should not be free to band together in an association as well as any other class of people in this Dominion. I know not why the Postmaster General spoke so unkindly of this association last session. It is a real association; it is not like the Consumers League in which the word "consumer's" should be spelled with possessive singular. Simply because the preceding government did not remedy this unsatisfactory condition of affairs is no reason why we on this side of the house should not advocate remedial action on the part of the government. The preceding government was tried by the electorate and in their opinion, found wanting, and discarded. In the very near future this government is going to be tried by the electorate, and already we can hear a "sound of going" in the tops of the mulberry trees. I suppose the Postmaster General might have his chauffeur drive him out into the country in his $8,000 Stutz car to meet the mail carriers and tell them they are prosperous.
I was very much impressed by the remarks of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). I am a little hard of hearing, but as I drive about the country I can always distinguish the rattle of the mail carrier's buggy. I see no reason why the rural mail carriers should be the only men in the service of the Post Office department to be stood up every four years and shot at. I believe the Deputy Postmaster General has had his salary raised by two thousand dollars during the past year, and yet when we ask for a modest increase and a permanency of employment with a few holidays for these men who go over the country roads in all weathers the Postmaster General turns a deaf ear to our request. But I am glad to see he is in a little more conciliatory mood this year than last. Perhaps he has been advised that the time is coming when the Prime Minister will be again reforming the senate and lowering the cost of living and the price of farm implements, and on that occasion no doubt the Postmaster General will be holding out to these mail carriers the bait of fair remuneration.
I should like the Postmaster General to make this clear. I understood' him to say that at the expiration of their contract letters

govern.

That was before 1921.

I am not yet clear as to
the number and type of rural mail carriers to whom the Postmaster General writes asking if they are prepared to carry on.
I cannot help you then.

I accept the Postmaster
General's word for the moment that only those against whom there has been no complaint as to their service-not their politics-are asked if they wish to carry on. I can name him a mail carrier in my riding with fifteen years' public service, against whom there was not a breath of complaint, but who was put up, his route advertised, and when the old and faithful servant and a new man tendered at the same figure, the Postmaster General's department wrote the defeated Liberal candidate asking who should get this contract, the old faithful servant or the new man. I think the Postmaster General has in mind the route in question.
Yes, I know the circumstances and will deal with the case when the time comes.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I do
not want to labour this question, having dealt with it rather fully last session. I feel that the rural mail carrier is entitled to a fair wage, to some guarantee of permanency of position, to holidays like any other civil servant, and to be treated as a human being. It seems to me that this is the only branch of his department where the Postmaster General can take a good fling at political patronage and declare "to the victor belongs the spoils." It has become an obsession with him, a plaything, and it would be unkind to deny him the little pleasure that this activity affords him.
As a basis of comparison let me take the letter carriers of the city of Toronto-and they are not overpaid. They get SI ,440, or thereabouts, a year delivering mail from house to house; their position is permanent; they are cared for if they lose their health in the service, and presumably they are entitled to a retiring allowance. At any rate, these men, with no more intelligence, no more capability and no better type of citizens than the rural mail carriers, get $1,440 a year to walk for a few hours twice a day over their routes, and then they are free to go back home; whereas the poor rural mail carrier has to cover up to 32 miles over the snow banks in the winter and through the mud roads in the spring and fall, keep up two horses-all for $590 a year on an average. Taking the Postmaster General's own figures, the average is even lower-only $500 a year.
I fail to understand why he should attempt to draw a red herring across the track by talking about bus and stage coach service. This amendment has to do definitely and clearly with the rural mail carrier. It may be, as the Postmaster General would say if he were speaking in another province, that this is another of "those fanatics from Ontario" who object to "G.R." being taken off the mail wagons. It is most unfair to say that the rural mail carrier makes any money carrying passengers. In my constituency I do not think there is a single rural mail carrier who makes $5 a year in this way. The average rural mail carrier goes down the concession and back, and he will give any man a free ride, even though this government has hiim working at a starvation wage. Let me give the Postmaster General an instance. And remember I have a great deal of appreciation for the Postmaster General in many respects. He has shown a broad sympathy and human kindness in many little matters in my constituency which I have brought to his notice. But I think he can hardly be cognizant of this. In the village of Auburn the post office was moved down the street 39 rods, which shortened the mail carrier's route by twice 39 rods, and the Postmaster General sent down a high paid inspector, getting perhaps $10 a day with travelling expenses, to measure that distance of 30 rods, and he docked that rural mail carrier $10.48 per annum for the rest of his term. That surely is proving that he is a friend of the working man in this country.

To give consideration to this question at this late date is not offering much consolation to those men who are doing the hardest work in the Postmaster General's department and getting the least pay. The Postmaster General will say, "Why, it is let by contract". Well, you know, a man gets settled down in one walk of life and he is afraid to get out of that groove lest he may not make a success of anything else; and if the Postmaster General's position were advertised to-night he would take a few thousands less in order to retain it.
I think it is worth a great deal more when I have to listen to such criticism as that.

Perhaps the truth hurts But let me tell the Postmaster General that he will continue to hear about it until this wrong is righted. So long as the poorest paid men do the hardest work in his department, receiving the least consideration, he is going to hear about the matter, and we are going to try to have him place the situation fairly before the house and not sidestep it by quoting bus line and stage coaches when he should be sticking to the plain rural mail carriers. The Postmaster General has not said that he would not accept his position at a few thousands less. Now a man has a rural mail contract and he is growing old He gave up his farm-and there are very few farmers in my constituency, not one out of ten, who carry mail. These rural mail carriers work steadily day by day. There is little else they can turn their hands to. And when their four years are up they may not be the ones to whom a letter is written-they may be of the wrong political stripe-asking them if they will carry on. The complaint has been registered that they voted U.F.O. in the last election and therefore they are put up at auction. The mail carrier is afraid he will lose his job. He has his horses and his rig and therefore he says, "I will tender a little less". If he is still able to exist, when the next four years expire he will tender again a little less. So that, as the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) said last year, the Postmaster Genera! will soon be getting this work done for practically nothing.
I would ask the Postmaster General to give one sane reason why these men in his service should be the only men who are made political toys of. Is there any reason? I have aeard the Postmaster General say that Canada has not lost one dollar through rural mail carriers, that they are honest, that they are efficient. [DOT] And it is the only branch of his

department of which he can so speak. Yet this is the way he proposes to reward honesty and efficiency. I know he has a particular grudge against a gentleman who went about striving to organize the rural mail carriers, a gentleman named McKinnon. The Postmaster General did not like it. He apparently thinks that the rural mail carriers did not know they were working too cheaply until Mr. McKinnon got a soap box and started a riot.
I wish once more to appeal to the Postmaster General to consider sane legislation in this matter, and to have the thoughts which he has in mind crystallized into legislation at least by next session so that these gentlemen can receive a fair wage according to the work that they are doing, instead of having ignominy cast upon them. Do not let the Postmaster General say to them, "You are the only gentlemen in my service who are not to receive the same treatment as others." I invite the Postmaster General now to come up to my constituency in his private car and send ahead his eight thousand dollar Stutz car, with chauffeur, and tell the people of that constituency that rural mail carriers or anybody else there are prosperous.
In closing I wish to say this. I feel that it is a blot on the fair name of Canada that we should meet many of the men carrying His Majesty's mail with the outfit they have. Last year I read in this house an account of a case in the city of Stratford where a rural mail carrier was taken before the court by the humane society for driving a horse which should not be driven. When Magistrate Makins learned that the Postmaster General was giving this man 81.75 a day to support that horse and rig and to maintain a family of five he dismissed the action. The same thing has occurred also in the vicinity of London.
Was not the party brought before the court, Fred Sitwell?

I do not know the name of the mail contractor. I read about the case in the Daily Beacon and I wrote to the magistrate to find out whether the newspaper clipping was correct and he sent me a letter enclosing the clipping and saying, "yes, it was absolutely correct."

The man brought before the court was not the mail contractor but the brother of the mail contractor who sold the contract to him at 8100 less than what he was getting from the government.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to add a few words to this discussion. In the first place let me say that I am entirely in sympathy with the great majority of the rural mail carriers throughout Canada who are asking for an improvement in their conditions, but I do not intend to be led astray by this plan of the hon. member 78594-104
for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), which is designed to embarrass me as well as many other supporters of the government.
If, as the hon. member suggests, these appointments should be under the Civil Service Commission, I must remember that a large number of the men at present employed in this work in my constituency would be out of a job. I understand that the age limit for applicants for civil service positions is thirty-five years, and this would shut out many of my friends.
Why could we not change that section of the Civil Service Act? That could be done in five minutes.

It would be some job. Then, as the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) has so well stated in his inimitable way, perhaps many of them would noit be able to answer satisfactorily the exacting questions which might be put by the examiners. A number of men possibly not so well qualified as others in an educational way would be quite capable of giving good service in this particular work. Other qualifications also are taken into account, and some older men who perhaps were not physically fit to serve in the war would be shut out.
Jso well-defined plan has been outlined by hon. gentlemen opposite for looking after the present incumbents of these positions, and therefore I think this proposed amendment is only an effort to embarrass the governm'ent. As I have already stated, these rural mail carriers give excellent service for small remuneration. Not long ago a large number of these men and women, because in our province I think some women carry on this work, met at, Charlottetown and placed their case before me. I promised to lay their representations before the government, and my colleague (Mr. Sinclair, Queens), the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) and myself have stated the case to the Postmaster General. It deserves serious consideration, and I am of the opinion that the government will be well advised to endeavour in some way to alleviate the difficulties under which many of these men labour. But, Mr. Speaker, to vote this government out of office and replace it with another in order to attain this end is, in my opinion, no solution of the difficulty.
I will tell my hon. friends and my supporters in the constituency which I have the honour to represent that I will support any reasonable measure intended to better the conditions of the rural mail carriers in Canada, but I prefer to have that matter attended to by the party to which I belong rather than by hon. gentlemen opposite.

Mr. Speaker, the post office is a
public utility, and no public utility in Canada should use its employees in the way the government uses these rural mail camera Where is the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan); what has he to say about this? According to a table appearing on page 12 of the report of the Post Office department this service was operated at a loss from 1868 to 1901; from then on, with the exception of a few years, it has shown a surplus. It is not creditable to the government to use the low-paid employees of this department in this way. Twenty-five years ago the section men on the railway were similarly treated; they were not permitted to join a union, but finally the railways had to give in. I take issue with the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Spotton) when he speaks of the city of Toronto. costing $8,000 or $10,000; no doubt this is a good way to provide work for the boys m the rural constituencies. Cowper's Task in that part called the Winter Evening, alludes to the low pay of rural mail delivery men in 1780 and 1790 when they received ten cents a day, and conditions have not improved much even in Canada since that time. I believe that all services should be on an equal basis and whether a man is sweeping the street, driving a tramcar or delivering rural mail, he is performing a service which is just as important as being the Prime Minister or the Postmaster General of this country. The other night the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) referred to the gentlemen who sit on the back rows of benches as the "back-benchers". It seems to be popular to coin catch phrases, but let me say that the branch of the public service which has been referred to as "that element" is doing as efficient a public service as is the Postmaster General and his deputy.

There should be a committee of the house appointed to go into these matters to see if we could not find a policy, as suggested by the amendment of the hon. member for South Wellington, whidh would bring about an improvement in the most important public service in Canada.
