Would the Postmaster General give the committee a general statement as to the air mail service?
Does the hon. gentleman wish the statement for the whole of Canada?
Yes.

Last year we had an air
mail service between Rimouski and Montreal. Montreal and Ottawa, and Ottawa and Toronto. That was twice a week to meet the incoming and outgoing British mail steamers. That continued during the season of navigation. During the winter time, after the close of navigation, we had an air mail service between Mai Bay, Seven Islands and Anticosti island:	That is a weekly service. After the
close of navigation we also had an air mail service between Moncton and the Magdalen islands. That service was begun a little later last winter than the winter before, but we carried it on until the opening of navigation or until sudh time as landing on the ice at the Magdalens became dangerous. I think we made seven or eight weekly trips. For a time we had an air mail service between Moncton and Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island. The ferry boat had been laid up on account of an accident and we could not get the mails in on the regular time, so the service was put on during that period. We also had a temporary mail service lasting about seven weeks between Ottawa and Montreal, Montreal and St. John, and St. John and Halifax. This was tried out with the object of establishing later on a regular route between Montreal and the maritime provinces. We also had an air mail service for ten days before Christmas and up to New Years between the principal points in the three western provinces, with Winnipeg

Supply-Post Office
as the starting point. That was done with the object of ascertaining the feasibility of establishing this year an air mail service route in the three western provinces.

There was no air mail
service from the east to Winnipeg?

No. Hon. gentlemen will
see that there is in the estimates an amount of $880,000. We intend establishing an air mail route from Toronto to Buffalo, connecting up at Windsor with the American lines and following those lines until we get to a point where we can join in again with our system at Winnipeg, and from Winnipeg continue the service over the three prairie provinces. The actual routes in the three prairie provinces have not yet been definitely determined, but one thing we are prepared to say, and that is that we will accommodate the larger cities and towns in those three provinces.
So far as an air mail service to the coast is concerned, I do not contemplate establishing any route this year because the surveys which the National Defence department have in hand for us have not yet been completed. When we intimate that we desire to establish an air mail service, the Department of National Defence undertake to have the route surveyed by their experts and to report to us on its feasibility. Part of that survey has been completed, and the remainder I hope will be done this year, so that we shall then be in a position to say when and how we may reach the Pacific coast.
We had other air mail services during the winter. We had a service from the head of steel out of Edmonton about 432 miles, up the Mackenzie river for some 700 miles. The people along that route used to receive their mail once during the winter, but with the service we gave them they received their mail pretty nearly once a week. We also had a service to the Flin-Flon area, to Cold lake. To-day our mail contractors in the Yukon have permission to use aeroplanes for the purpose of carrying out their contracts.

Is there an air mail
service to the Yukon?

The contractors in the
Yukon have permission to use aeroplanes ii they so desire. We have other air mail services, but not directly under the control of the department. For instance, a company developing some part of the country will ask permission to carry mail, and we give them permission to use what is called the sticker system; that is, they would carry the mail, protecting it by the sticker system, and they
could charge to those who wished to send their mail in that way a certain fee. We regulated the fee. In some cases it was 10 cents per ounce, and the highest charge was 20 cents per ounce. That, Mr. Chairman, is a rough outline of what we are doing and what we are hoping to do this year in the air mail service.

I notice in the
press that in all probability the air mail service between Montreal and Toronto will be discontinued. Is the department considering that?

made the statement myself that if the business men and commercial houses and those engaged in industry did not sufficiently appreciate what the department was doing as a convenience to them and as an extension of our mail system to patronize the service as it should be patronized, I did not intend to run it for the health of the department. I felt that cities like Toronto and Montreal having that service should appreciate it to the extent that we would at least meet expenses. The matter rests there.
